articles.text: Cost overrun soars to 79 percent The Piedmont City Council approved at their meeting on Monday, December 2, an additional $2.8 million in funding to complete the new community pool. The money will come primarily from the City’s Facilities Capital Fund. This action brings the total project cost to $34.9 million, an increase of 79 percent from the original bond of $19.5 million approved by voters as Measure UU in November 2020. Since construction started in early 2023, the project has incurred significant new costs due to: • Project delays related to weather, utilities, and the discovery of two buried fuel tanks on the construction site • Additional costs associated with the complexity of pool electrification • Soil disposal, due to the presence of naturally occurring arsenic in the soil composition Additional costs have also come from construction adjacent to the pool site, including waterproofing of the Recreation Department building and the full-width repaving of Magnolia Avenue. George Sanen, Construction Manager on the project, expects construction on the sidewalk of Magnolia Avenue to be done by late January. Completion of the Magnolia sidewalk is dependent on PG&E submerging a gas line 12-16 inches lower. Pool architect Clarence Mamuyac speaking to City Council. Joining the meeting remotely was Griffin Construction President Jon Hughes (left) and Construction Manager George Sanen (right).

Learning from John the Baptist By Rev. Jim Hopkins “And the crowds asked John, ‘What, then should we do?’” Luke 3:7-18 John the Baptist was a star. Crowds followed him. Rulers feared him. Seekers of truth revered him. If there had been paparazzi in his day, they would have stalked him. History remembers John kindly. Every third Sunday of Advent we read about him. We remember that his name means “God is gracious.” We remember that he preached and baptized in the wilderness. We remember that he fulfilled his mission to “Prepare the way of the Lord.” We remember that Jesus came to him for baptism. Beyond being fascinated by this powerful, complex and courageous individual, we do well to think about ways we can participate in his work of preparing a way for Jesus to be known in our lives and in our world. John did that work well but it did not end with him. It continues even now. Paying attention to what the gospel of Luke tells us about John’s words and deeds gives us some good ideas for ways in which we can prepare the way for Jesus to come into our world. The first thing John did was to go into the wilderness. This may mean that we need to get outside and appreciate nature. It can also mean that we can start preparing the way for Jesus by finding a quiet place, even if that quiet place is in our hearts and minds. We live in a noisy world. We prepare the way by literally, and figuratively, turning down the noise. The second thing John did was to ask the crowd that found him in the wilderness “What brings you here? Who warned you to flee the coming judgment?” In so doing, he teaches us that we prepare the way by considering carefully who and what we are listening to. What are the influences that shape us? What are the values that guide us? What are the teachings that form us? Who are the voices that call us? These are central questions in our work of preparing a way for Jesus. The third thing John did was to respond to the question “What then should we do?” He urged the people to share their possessions and not exploit others financially. He made it clear that we prepare the way for Jesus by caring about the well-being of others in tangible, helpful, “meet their basic needs” kinds of ways. We prepare the way for Jesus by making sure that our spiritual values are expressed in physical realities. This Advent, as we consider the ways in which John fulfilled his purpose, let us commit ourselves to preparing the way for Jesus. Rev. articles.text: The Piedmont Post asked Teachers Union President Elise Marks about the false report of a gunman outside the high school on November 12. Though later deemed to be a hoax it resulted in students and staff being put on lockdown for around 50 minutes. That event has since been overshadowed with the tragedy of three former PHS students being killed in an auto accident on November 27. But to not be forgotten, Marks describes the events from inside a Piedmont classroom when fear struck Piedmont campuses. – Elise Marks, Pres., PHS Teachers Union “The awful accident and loss of three Piedmont High graduates the day before Thanksgiving obviously eclipsed everything else,” Marks began. The following is Marks’ account of the lockdown on November 12 when a gunman was reported to be outside of Piedmont High School. Dr. Marks’ statement “Teachers got an email at 12:06 p.m. saying that a “shelter in place” was about to be initiated, but there was no detail given at the time. An announcement came over the loudspeaker right after that to go into shelter in place. Shelter in place is what we use when there might be a threat near the school so that we keep kids in our classrooms. It’s usually more for things like a gas leak a couple blocks away or something like that. We do lock our doors, close our windows and lower our blinds, and keep voices in the room quiet and tell kids they can’t go out to the bathroom. But we continue teaching, very quietly. Teachers were actually texting each other to double-check that we all knew what the protocols were. My classroom is right by the breezeway and when the first email alert came through, I locked my classroom door behind me so the kids were safe and ran a couple of steps into the hallway to pull the outside door closed and cut off access to the building. At that point, through the door windows, I could see a group of maybe half a dozen Piedmont police in tight formation hurrying onto campus. There were no other signs of trouble, so I hurried back into my classroom. On the teacher text chain, I’m seeing someone at 12:11 saying that “it’s a real warning from PPD,” but clearly not everyone An empathy board allowed students to add post-it notes about the experience of the school being on lockdown on November 12 under the fear of a gunman on campus. saw that text. I’m not sure how much time passed, maybe more than five minutes, before a second announcement came over the loudspeaker that this was now a “lockdown.” That’s the signal that there’s imminent threat on campus, presumably an active shooter. As soon as we knew it was lockdown, everyone moved fast. We’ve rehearsed this a lot, so it literally took just seconds for most students to shove desks aside and get down into the safest spot in the classroom, while a few volunteers and I quickly piled desks and stools in front of the door and used a trick we’ve learned to immobilize the door handle from the inside. Everyone was silent the entire time, not even a brief exclamation or questions to me about what to do. Somehow kids did manage to slide their phones from the phone holder, so they had them and were texting friends and family. At this point, we didn’t know what the threat was, though it was clear this wasn’t a drill. It was maybe another ten minutes before I saw the text alert from the police that a report had come in that said someone with an AR-15 was in front of the PHS Main Office threatening harm. That was definitely a frightening moment, seeing those actual words. But we all imagine this scenario enough that it wasn’t really a shock. We knew we were as safe as we could manage to be and that it was very unlikely that anyone could make it through the door. Everyone stayed very quiet. I texted teachers at Havens to see if they were in lockdown, but they weren’t. I also silently motioned kids to really squish together to be in the absolute safest part of the room to minimize the chance that if bullets were to come in through the door or windows that anyone would be in the direct line of fire. That’s an awful, awful thing to have to be calculating, but it’s something all teachers have to think about. At 12:37, we got the follow-up message that “This appears to be a wide-spread ‘swatting’ event across the county, but out of caution PMS, MHS, and PHS are in lockdown while the school is searched.” So we had to stay crouched and silent waiting for the all-clear, which we got via PUSD email at 12:47, though the police alert confirming it went out at 12:52, and we all decided on the text chain that we’d just stay put until we heard an official announcement over the PA, which came a few minutes later. So the whole thing lasted almost 50 minutes from our perspective. Kids seemed calm afterwards, but maybe it’s just being resigned. I gave them a few minutes to talk with each other and have a chance to get some water or use the bathroom. After that, it seemed like the best thing to do was just continue with the rest of class as if it was normal. At 1:03, someone said they heard a chopper circling. The next day someone posted a sign on a bulletin board in the STEAM building hallway where students could leave their thoughts on Post It notes. Some kids wrote notes about how scared they felt and how terrible it is that kids in school have to worry about this. We should have done more to help kids process it, but honestly even the adults don’t know what to say. We reacted fast to maximize safety, and everyone did that well.

articles.text: Piedmont Girl Scouts brought cheer and plenty of holiday crafts inspiration to the tree lighting ceremony on Wednesday night, December 4. Beach Elementary 3rd Grade Brownie Troop 30981 and Piedmont 10th grade Senior Girl Scouts Troop 30713 set up a 20-foot long row of tables for making crafts and decorate holiday ornaments. Nearly 100 people wrote messages of kindness and positivity to hang as ornaments for the Senior Girl Scouts tree. It was part of their troop’s Take Action Project with a ‘Make the World A Brighter Place’ themed activity. The Brownie Girl Scouts are also working towards their “Take Action” Journey Badge and hosted a craft table for younger children to decorate a star, wreath or snowflake ornament or puppet. By the end of the evening, kids attending the event had made more than 100 pieces of artwork to take home. “I loved seeing all the little kids and helping them out,” said Brownie Troop member, Maeve Denison. Beach Brownie troop members Elena Dean (left), Maeve Denison, Lucia Jones & Essie Brezovec. Elena Dean (left) and Maeve Denison help a younger child use a glue gun for an ornament. The Senior Girl Scouts tree is adorned with messages from community members. “It was fun to see kids making up their own ideas,” said Troop member Essie Brezovec. All the materials were provided by the troops, with members planning and procuring the supplies in advance. “I’m enjoying all the activities for the kids,” said Anarjhya Vardhani, whose 2-year-old daughter, Ehime, glued sequins onto a star ornament. “It allows kids to exercise their creativity and I love that the Girl Scouts are running it. It shows great leadership on their part.” Piedmont High School sophomore Skye Baack, a member of Troop 30713 said that she and some of her fellow troop members have been participating in Piedmont’s holiday lights ceremonies since they were in Kindergarten. “I loved being able to share activities with the kids and do things together we find enjoyable,” she said. Being a role model for younger Girl Scouts was one of the highlights of the experience, she added. The 8- and 9-year olds in the Beach Brownie Troop were equally thrilled to be included in the event for the first time and help the community alongside the older Girl Scouts. “I really liked that all the Girl Scouts were working together,” said Brownie Troop member, Elena Dean. “It was really fun.”
articles.title: Girl Scout Troops lead the way with craft-making

articles.text: We’ve all done it: someone’s talking to us, and we’re nodding along, but we’re thinking about something completely different— like what’s for dinner or how we’ll escape this conversation to refill our drink. Sure, we heard them, but did we actually listen? As we head into the holiday season – family dinners, parties, gatherings – it’s easy to show up physically while staying checked out mentally. And yet, this is also the time of year when many people feel the most alone or isolated, even in a room full of people. Why? Because there’s a difference between being around people who hear you and people who actually listen to you. Hearing is the easy part. Hearing is passive. It’s the sound waves hitting your ears and your brain saying, “Yep, I caught that.” You hear the background music, the hum of conversation, and that one uncle who always talks a little too loudly. But hearing doesn’t mean you’re engaging. You can hear someone and still miss the point entirely—or worse, miss the person entirely. But the real gift is listening! Listening is active. It’s intentional. It’s the effort of tuning in, not just to someone’s words but to their meaning, their feelings, their humanity. When you listen, you’re saying, “I see you. I value what you have to say.” And let’s be honest: isn’t that what we all want, especially during the holidays? To feel seen and understood, even amidst the chaos of the season? How to Really Listen This Holiday Season Want to be the person who makes someone feel like they truly belong at the table? Here’s how to step up your listening game: 1. Put Down Your Phone: This one’s a no-brainer, but it’s harder than it sounds. Give the gift of your undivided attention. 2. Pause and Be Present: Before responding, take a beat. Listen not just to what they’re saying, but why they’re saying it. 3. Notice What’s Unsaid: Sometimes it’s about the tone, the hesitation, or the look in their eyes. Pay attention to the emotions behind the words. 4. Ask Thoughtful Questions: Show you care by asking questions that go deeper. “What’s been the best part of your year so far?” hits differently than, “How’s work?” 5. Reflect Back: Once you listen to what they say, reflect it
articles.title: The difference between listening and hearing

articles.text: On Tuesday, December 17, at 6:30 p.m. a thought-provoking film centering on mathematics in the modern world will be shown in Alan Harvey Theater. The showing of the 91-minute film Counted Out is open to the public, and will include comments from its filmmaker, Vicki Abeles. articles.text: Piedmont Makers hosted a 2-day weekend of robotics events at Piedmont Middle School on December 7 and 8 with over 600 students and 150 parent coaches. Starting with the LEGO League Explore Festival on Saturday, the tournament continued on Sunday with the LEGO League Challenge Community Tournament. The LEGO League Explore Festival is an annual event for children ages six to ten to learn about STEAM (science, technology, engineering, arts, and math) through hands-on activities and challenges. At the festival, teams made presentations on a project related ocean exploration. They shared their LEGO models for their project solution, including code. “The LEGO League Explore Festival is a way to showcase the incredible creativity and problem-solving of our young teams. The teamwork is definitely the hardest part!” said Piedmont Makers Explore Co-commissioner Marta Lutsky. “We hope that this event will inspire the next generation of engineers and scientists.” This year’s festival set alltime records for participation and attendance, with 56 teams and over 500 attendees visiting Piedmont Middle School’s Buzz Redford Gymnasium on Saturday. According to event organizer Scott Miller, it was the biggest weekend in Piedmont Makers Robotics history. On Sunday, 35 LEGO League Challenge teams and 250 students took over the Middle School campus, filling the Redford Gym, Morrison Gym, several classrooms and the school plaza for judging during a full day of robotic competition. The LEGO League Challenge Community Tournament is a robotics competition for children ages nine to fourteen. Teams of up to eight kids design, build, and program LEGO robots to autonomously complete a series of challenges in a 2.5-minute match. The robots “The Ocean Explorers” from Beach Elementary School describe their LEGO model to a project judge. The “Axolotl Stars” from Beach Elementary and their coaches show off their ocean-themed project poster. Over 100 parent volunteers take part in mentoring and guiding teams throughout the fall season. The “Penguin Powerbots” from Wildwood Elementary, pose with their robot before showing it to a judge. The team later won the “Champion Award”, the top-prize of the weekend. The festival also included hands-on activities. Here, a team member shows off a day-of mechanical creation built from some of the thousands of LEGO Technic bricks that were available for free building. Students use visual code blocks from the Scratch programming language to learn the fundamental principles of software engineering as ages as young as kindergarten. The “Happy Robots” from Rheem Elementary in Moraga built a multistory model highlighting the layers of ocean exploration.

articles.text: Piedmont High’s boys’ basketball team finished in third place at the annual Winter Classic, now hosted by the Highlanders for the 34th time. In the tournament. PHS defeated Envision Academy 74-36 in the first round on Thursday, December 5, followed by an 85-58 loss to Acalanes in the semifinals. They won third place with a 59-52 victory over HeadRoyce on Saturday, December 7. Northgate wound up winning this year’s Winter Classic by beating Acalanes. Piedmont’s win over Head-Royce was with a Division 4 North Coast Section foe. “We now have two D4 wins, which already sets us up nicely for NCS [post-season playoffs]. Because we’re in the league we’re in, you never know how things are going to go against those big, physical schools,” Although the Highlanders loss to Acalanes was by 27 points, they were in the game through three quarters, including an 11 point disadvantage early in the third quarter. PHS returned the following night to play stout defense for the win against the Jayhawks. “We’re young, so you’re going to see flashes of brilliance and times that we’re going to struggle. In terms of a loss like that, any time you come back and get a good win against a well-coached team, it’s a sign of growth for a young team,” Spencer said. It was a big performance on Saturday night for junior guard Dillon Casey, scoring 28 points. articles.text: Staff Photos Nathan Bekele (left) celebrates with Jacques Saldanha after scoring the game-winning goal against Granada in the last minute. Piedmont’s boys’ soccer team pulled off a stunning 1-nil victory over Granada on Thursday, December 5 under the lights at Witter Field. In the final minute of the game junior Nathan Bekele scored the game-winner at the very end of regulation time The victory came against a team that reached the Division 1 North Coast Section playoffs last season. “First, it’s great to have all the players back from [their club teams]. It’s significant to have the seniors in the starting lineup. It’s great for the boys to get the win, but there’s still work to be done,” coach Ben Russell said. On the game-winning goal, Max Goldfarb sent a long free kick from about 50 yards away from the goal. His long pass sailed past Jacques Saldanha soaking up defensive pressure, bouncing off of the turf and perfectly for Bekele to head in the ball. Nathan had just entered the game as a substitute just a few minutes before scoring the winner. “We got a free kick and I just got into the game. The ball came flying and I managed to get my head on it. It was a good confidence booster,” Bekele said. “I knew it was going to be the last play of the game. I just made a run and I thought the ball was coming my way. I was right under it and the ball went over me, then I saw Nathan and his head was down. It bounced off of his head and goes in the goal, it was an act of God,” Saldanha recalled of the play. It was also a sentimental moment for the Highlanders following the tragic passing of former soccer players Soren Dixon and Jack Nelson. Saldanha, now a senior, was a sophomore on the squad when Dixon and Nelson were seniors. “It’s been a really hard week for the Piedmont community. We lost two amazing former players. That was the kind of goal Soren and Jack would’ve scored; they were the most clutch players and scored goals just like that. I made countless memories with them,” Saldanha reflected. top for an attempt on target, but Granada’s keeper did well to rush off his line to make the stop. articles.text: The San Francisco Gay Men’s Chorus will perform its annual Holiday Spectacular! at Zellerbach Hall in Berkeley on Saturday, December 21. The San Francisco Gay Men’s Chorus is the world’s first openly gay chorus most often credited with creating the LGBT choral movement. The iconic ensemble will sing traditional holiday classics like “Little Drummer Boy,” “Sleigh Ride,” and “Deck the Halls” as well as holiday pop songs by George Michael, the Jackson 5, and the Manhattan Transfer for this Bay Area annual celebration. Beyond caroling, the evening will include satirical sketches, ugly Christmas sweaters, Santa outfits, and guest dancers and drag artists. Performance begins at 5 p.m. Call the Cal Performances box office at 510-642-9988 or visit https://calperformances.org to purchase tickets. The San Francisco Gay Men’s Chorus

articles.text: Baroque New Year’s Eve at the Opera American Bach Soloists will return to the Herbst Theatre in San Francisco to perform an evening of Baroque pieces on New Year’s Eve, December 31. The program includes instrumental masterpieces by G.F Handel, J.P Rameau and C.H Graun performed by talented musicians, playing alongside soprano Maya Kherani and countertenor Eric Jurenas. Kherani recently showcased her debut with the New York Philharmonic in Handel’s Messiah, and Jurenas was an American Bach Soloist in 2011 where he sang the roles of Polinesso, Duke of Albany, in Handel’s Ariodante. The soloists are led by Artistic Director Jeffrey Thomas, recognized globally as a leading interpreter of Bach and Baroque music. Thomas co-founded American Bach Soloists in 1989 with the mission of introducing today’s audiences to Bach’s famous cantatas. The concert begins at 4 p.m. well before the midnight hour so guests will have opportunities to attend festivities afterward. articles.text: Evening and afternoon performances at Zellerbach Hall this weekend Dorrance Dance, an awardwinning tap dance company based in New York City, will perform the classic Nutcracker Suite at Zellerbach Hall in Berkeley on December 14 and 15. articles.text: Dr. Suess’s greatest children’s stories come to life on the Berkeley Playhouse stage in the whimsical musical Seussical, performing through December 22. Directed by William Thomas Hodgson and choreographed by Leslie Waggoner, the musical is a collection of the writer’s most loved stories including Cat in the Hat, The Lorax and Horton Hears a Who. “I have such a fondness for this show,” said Berkeley Playhouse Artistic Director Kimberly Dooley. “I directed William in our production of Seussical in 2011 when he performed as Cat in the Hat. It’s an absolute delight to see him come full circle and get to be in the director’s seat.” Dooley added that the characters and cast this year “are zany and vibrant, and there are some really heartfelt moments that leave you feeling inspired.” Some cast members have family members performing, making Suessical “an intergenerational musical,” she said. The cast includes Stephen Kanaski as Cat in the Hat, Christian Arteaga as Horton the Elephant, No’Eau Kahalekulu as Gertrude McFuzz, and Andrea Rae as Mayzie La Bird. Hodgson said the musical is about “real deep human issues” that can be felt by all ages. “This is a family show, it’s a holiday show, it’s a feel-good show, it is a raucous show,” he said. “There’s a lot of dancing and colors and interaction.” Performances run Friday through Sunday and select weekday evenings. For tickets or more information, call the box office at (510) 845-8542 x351 or visit berkeleyplayhouse.org to purchase online.

articles.text: San Francisco Playhouse’s newest production Waitress is playing onstage now through January 18. Susi Damilano’s revision of the motion picture Waitress, written by Adrienne Shelly, features music and lyrics by pop singer-songwriter Sara Bareilles. The play first premiered in 2015 at the American Repertory Theater in Cambridge, Massachusetts, and then transferred to Broadway in 2016, where it went on to receive 3 Tony Award nominations including Best Musical and Best Original Score. Waitress features protagonist Jenna, a diner waitress and expert pie maker, who is stuck in a small town and a loveless marriage. Jenna worries she will have to abandon her dream of opening her own bakery when she becomes unexpectedly pregnant, until she enters a baking contest and meets the soon-to-be love of her life. Ruby Day plays Jenna, and is supported by Zeke Edmonds, who plays Jenna’s love interest, Dr. Pomatter. Supporting characters include Louis Parnell, Dorian Lockett, Tanika Baptiste and Sharon Shao. Music Direction is by Dave Dobrusky and choreography by Nicole Helfer. Waitress is playing at San Francisco Playhouse through January 18, 2025. The venue is located at 450 Post Street in the heart of San Francisco’s Union Square theatre district. Performances are Tuesday through Sunday. Visit https://www.sfplayhouse. org/sfph/2024-2025-season/waitress/ to purchase tickets. Through December 28, families can book a reservation to sip steaming pots of fine loose-leaf tea with house-made scones and fruit-topped pastries. Christmas tree in Golden Gate Park Christmas tree in Golden Gate Park The San Francisco Recreation and Park Department kicked off the holiday season on December 5 with its annual tree-lighting event in Golden Gate Park. Affectionately called “Norton” or “Uncle John’s tree,” in honor of Golden Gate Park’s designer and first park superintendent John McLaren, the 135-year old Monterey cypress in front of McLaren Lodge is once again adorned with 550 colorful holiday bulbs. The annual tree-lighting might be San Francisco’s oldest holiday tradition. articles.text: Let’s get in our Time Machine once again. You’re already thinking about Archimedes, but that was not the inspiration for this article. It was partially Richard Halliburton‘s “Complete Book of Marvels”. But that is only part of the story. Let’s go back in time to 1848 when President Polk initiated the Gold Rush. Prior to that time California was a very quiet, beautiful place to live. And then more than 300,000 people came to California looking for riches from the gold mines. There were no taxes and everything you found was absolutely free. Sacramento and San Francisco were the focus of everything that happened. In 1848 San Francisco had approximately 200 residents (or 1000, depending on your source). The population increased to 36,000 residents overnight. Sacramento’s story is almost the same. Both cities are fascinating because they are beautiful and historically important. Sadly, very little remains of what once was. In San Francisco historically important neighborhoods such as the Fillmore and Chinatown have changed dramatically over the years. Halliburton is very romantic when he describes in his book places such as the Golden Gate Bridge, the Bay Bridge, and Treasure Island. Take a half-day trip to Sacramento’s Old Town. Virtually all of the buildings were boarded up and in disrepair… a classic Skid Row in every aspect. And then someone came up with the idea to rejuvenate it – and they did. articles.text: Visit historic Filoli House and Garden in Woodside now through January 12 to see the 16-acre estate decorated for the holidays. Filoli’s team has installed and decorated 22 trees, 3,600 light strands that stretch more than 18 miles, with more than 7,000 luminescent ornaments, and 1,000 feet of festive garlands. The Reception Room’s 18-foot ceiling creates an appropriate location for “The Grand Tree,” the tallest tree on display. The two-story historic mansion contains 56 rooms, including a ballroom and reception room designed to host concerts and debutante balls. Each room in the mansion is adorned with holiday decorations that complement the room’s original hues and aesthetics. The design team carefully recreated the original holiday placement used by Agnes and William Bourn, Filoli’s first owners. Original artifacts can be viewed throughout the home. Lurline Roth, who lived with her family in the mansion after the Bourns, was an avid collector of religious icons. Her Italian Murano glass nativity scene is now on display in the study. While holiday evenings at Filoli are truly a sight to see, the lighting enhancements glow just as festively during the day. Daytime admission allows visitors to explore the estate trail before sundown and admire the garden’s autumnal colors. Daytime hours are 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. The estate is open until 9 p.m. through January. To learn more about holidays at Filoli and to purchase tickets, visit https://filoli.org/events/holidays/. articles.text: Everlasting Moments is a remarkable film, unhurried and beautifully photographed: warm sepia images contrasted by stark winter scenes; a trolly car emerges out of the mist on a dark winter’s night; a summer picnic, lush and green and blue; the harrowing shadow of an enormous zeppelin floating overhead, darkening the neighborhood; a young woman, on a bitterly cold day, enveloped by slanting sunlight, walks out onto the thin ice, only to disappear into the fog; the face of Maria Larsson, briefly caught in agony is transformed as she finds resolve. It’s breathtaking. From beginning to end, Everlasting Moments is Swedish director and cinematographer Jan Troell’s film. Now 78, after 40 years of moviemaking, Troell has created a lovely, episodic, quietly told narrative set in the early 1900s. Mar ia Larsson (Mar ia Heiskanen), Finnish, marries Sigfrid (Mikael Persbrandt) and moves to Maimo, Sweden. Just prior to her marriage she wins a Contessa folding camera in a lottery and rather than sell it, she puts it away in a keepsake trunk. Only years later – now with children, coping with Sigfrid’s drunken episodes and abusive rages – does she remember the camera and takes it to a local studio to sell. At the shop she meets Sebastian Pedersen, proprietor, who encourages her to keep the Maria Heiskanen in Everlasting Moments camera and take pictures. Maria soon discovers that she has an eye. A new world is suddenly revealed and captured. Pedersen, looking at her pictures, tells her, “If you’re a person who sees, you have no choice but to do so.” The connection between them – her sensitivity and openness and his kindness and generosity – is palatable yet by unspoken agreement held in check. And so, like an undeveloped print dropped into a tray of solution, Everlasting Moments comes into focus. Slowly. Deliberately. Evocatively. Through seemingly pedestrian moments, the picture is brought into unyielding relief. It is a gorgeous thing to behold, subtle, nuanced and deeply human. The performances, led by Heiskanen and Persbrandt and Christensen, are so wonderfully rendered it becomes impossible to comprehend that they are acting. The verisimilitude of their circumstances is seamlessly convincing while Troell explores the resilience of love, the abrasive effect of resentment, even loathing, and the courage that is required of a woman who, constrained by the dictates of a narrow and fiercely judgmental world, manages to step forward and find herself. What Troell asks of the audience is to find a reflection of the human condition. He asks us to see, while never allowing sentiment or caricature to overwhelm the story. His film has a fragile yet enduring honesty. This is film as art, and is the work of a master. Everlasting Moments. Starring Maria Heiskanen, Jesper Christensen, Mikael Persbrandt and Ghita Norby. Directed by Jan Troell. Swedish with subtitles. 1 hr., 32 min. Not rated. Streaming on prime/apple tv. Released in 2017. articles.text: I’m reluctant to say that The Ghost Writer is the antidote to those fast-paced, intense “B” thrillers that are ever ubiquitous. Recent examples would be The Hurt Locker, The Green Zone, as well as the Bourne trilogy, all shot with the revolutionary handheld steadicam and the digital Red, creating a grainy, documentary style, jerky and intense – a gestalt of visual experience. Antidote is too strong a word, perhaps, even a bit disparaging of a genre that is superbly entertaining. The Ghost Writer, directed by Roman Polanski, does possess all of the intensity of a thriller; however, the narrative is conveyed not by action and physical confrontation, but through dialogue. This is a film of language, well written, with engaging set pieces wherein the characters reveal themselves and the plot – which is at first intriguing and then ever more complex. Told from the point of view of a thirty-something writer (Ewan McGregor) for hire (his name is never given. He’s referred to only as “Ghost” or “man”) who reluctantly agrees to edit the memoirs of Adam Lang (Pierce Brosnan), England’s recently resigned Prime Minister. Lang is now living in a stark, contemporary house on Martha’s Vineyard – the month is January, it’s cold, the sky and ocean a mix of wintry slate and teal, rain falling constantly. Everything feels ominous and unsettling; exactly Ewan McGregor in The Ghost Writer

articles.text: Secretariat is a Disney film about a magnificent chestnut racehorse nicknamed Big Red, also known as Secretariat, thought by some to be the greatest racehorse of all time. In 1973, Red won, against all odds, the Triple Crown: the Kentucky Derby, the Preakness and the Belmont Stakes. It was then, and remains still, the Holy Grail of horse racing, a trifecta that is rarely attained. No one does movies about animals better than Disney and Secretariat is filled with excitement: tight shots of jockeys clutching the reins as horses weighing some 1,200 pounds charge around an oval track more than a mile long. It’s intense, even thrilling. Of course, it’s irresistible for Disney not to give Secretariat a sentient intelligence. In one scene, Penny Chenery (Diane Lane), owner of Secretariat, stands holding the horse’s bridle, looking the horse in the eyes, while he looks back and conveys to Penny that he’s ready to race. Along with windows which we discussed last time, doors make up the most common component of fenestration – the collective term for openings in the architecture of a building. Since the most prominent fenestration of a building is generally the entry side, it includes the most important door in the building, the entry door. This door and its place in the facade composition are essential elements of the style and quality of the entire building. Often “nested” in an architectural recess, the entry door likely includes architectural enhancements like surrounding tile work or plaster accentuation, and usually closely surrounding windows of various types. Among these are sidelights, which are vertical fixed (non-operable) windows adjacent to a door, and transoms which are horizontal windows above the door. Besides the door leaf (the actual hinged panel), the style, size and finish of hardware including locks, hinges, thresholds, stops, weather stripping, and address numbers are also important visual considerations for the appropriateness and quality of the door(s). (In a previous column on Porches and Entries, we mentioned a number of other components that work with the door itself to make a welcoming entry.) The process of designing door assemblies can be fairly complex. Desired swing direction (door “handing”) must be coordinated Doors and windows are always related on a building’s fenestration, especially at the main entry. Very different in scale, style and materials, both the traditional and contemporary designs shown in these Piedmont homes are well done. Note the deep recesses on the traditional (top left photo), and the matching door/stair rail material on the contemporary (top right photo). In this Craftsman style home, I would say the visually strong and nicely proportioned porch opening could also be considered a part of the architectural fenestration. Nicely proportioned and detailed, well designed garage doors such as these can be considered a fenestration feature on a home. articles.text: Wednesday, December 4 was a beautiful, sunny, winter morning. During 2024 the Walking on Wednesdays group hadn’t gotten to Olive Avenue on the southwest side of town, so that was the day’s destination. Along the way, there was some Key System train history on Fairview Avenue to be shared too. Forty-two walkers and two K-9 best friends were at the Exedra to enjoy it all. The walkers went on Fairview and stopped for a group photo in front of a Victorian home built in 1896. Some history of the Key System was told. The transit system (bus, streetcar) began service in 1903 in Berkeley and in 1904 in what was to become the City of Piedmont. The No. 12 Line was originally called the “Grand Avenue & Hollis Street Line.” It initially went along a set of Oakland and Piedmont streets including Oakland, Fairview, Grand, Webster, 14th, Market, 24th, Adeline, 32nd, and Hollis to Yerba Buena. This line began on Grand and Wildwood Avenues, at Piedmont’s boundary, as a shuttle to Perry Street near where Oakland Avenue and the MacArthur Freeway are today. The line connected there with the Lakeshore Avenue line cars. The end of the line was extended from Grand up Fairview in 1915. The route had a few name changes over the years, but in 1928 its name was finalized as the “No. 12” line. However, on June 27, 1948 the No. 12 Grand Avenue streetcar service was abandoned, and buses replaced the streetcars. The group walked down Fairview past a long street median that was once a Key System right-of-way. They crossed Grand Avenue and climbed up Sunnyside to Olive Avenue where they enjoyed seeing many front yard gardens. Olive goes along the top edge of the Morcom Rose Garden below. The garden is in a 7.5- acre, natural bowl in Oakland, but when the City of Oakland purchased the site in 1911 the best park entrance was through land in Piedmont. The Piedmont City Council joined the effort to create the park by acquiring Piedmont lots at the southern corner of Olive and Oakland Avenues. The walkers went up Olive and passed a garage that is decorated as a bar with a sign proclaiming it to be “Tom’s Tavern Steak House.” The group crossed the Oakland Avenue bridge that Albert Farr designed in 1910 as a significant entrance to Piedmont. The bridge replaced a wood trestle that was built in 1890 for the cable cars that served what was to become Piedmont. Farr used the same Spanish design that he used for Piedmont City Hall. The bridge was built in 1911 as a reinforced concrete arch bridge over Linda Avenue with a 160- foot arch span and a total length of 343 feet. The relatively new lampposts and lights make the bridge a lovely entrance to the city, and guardrails make it safer for walkers. The improvements were made by the city in 2014. The walkers crossed Grand Avenue to Arbor Drive, where they discovered a hidden, 110- foot path between Arbor Drive and MacKinnon Place and Magnolia Avenue. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Register at https://tinyurl. com/3ethkehu. articles.text: The Rhone wine region of France is usually broken into two sub-regions, the North and the South. The north extends from just south of Orange to Valence and primarily focuses on the Syrah grape for reds and the Viognier and Marsanne grape for whites. I recently wrote an article focusing on the wines of the North region, so this month I will be focusing on the South region. It is a much harder task as the South Rhone region is huge compared to the north and produces a staggering number of wines. It ranges from Valence all the way down to the Mediterranean Sea. As the Rhone River progresses southward, the valley widens and the climate changes. The region is distinctly more Provencal with a Mediterranean influence in culture and climate. The summers are long and warm and the winters are mild. Rainfall is less than in the north and the famous Mistral wind is a major player. Another unique characteristic of these wines are the nuances of Garrigue – the wild resinous herbs that cover the landscape. If Syrah is the big boy of the North Grenache is king in the South and forms the foundation of the areas popular blends. You’ll also encounter Mourvedre, Cinsault, Counoise, Carignan, Grenache Blanc, Marsanne, Roussanne, Clairette, Bourboulenc and a host of minor players. The Southern Rhone’s most famous wine is Chateauneufdu-Pape, a blend containing up to 19 varieties of wine grapes as permitted by AOC rules. pages.text: 22 Wednesday, December 11, 2024 The Wine Corner Some stars from Southern Rhone region By Pierre DuMont The Rhone wine region of France is usually broken into two sub-regions, the North and the South. The north extends from just south of Orange to Valence and primarily focuses on the Syrah grape for reds and the Viognier and Marsanne grape for whites. I recently wrote an article focusing on the wines of the North region, so this month I will be focusing on the South region. It is a much harder task as the South Rhone region is huge compared to the north and produces a staggering number of wines. It ranges from Valence all the way down to the Mediterranean Sea. As the Rhone River progresses southward, the valley widens and the climate changes. The region is distinctly more Provencal with a Mediterranean influence in culture and climate. The summers are long and warm and the winters are mild. Rainfall is less than in the north and the famous Mistral wind is a major player. Another unique characteristic of these wines are the nuances of Garrigue – the wild resinous herbs that cover the landscape. If Syrah is the big boy of the North Grenache is king in the South and forms the foundation of the areas popular blends. You’ll also encounter Mourvedre, Cinsault, Counoise, Carignan, Grenache Blanc, Marsanne, Roussanne, Clairette, Bourboulenc and a host of minor players. The Southern Rhone’s most famous wine is Chateauneufdu-Pape, a blend containing up to 19 varieties of wine grapes as permitted by AOC rules. The other major AOC’s of the area are Gigondas, Lirac, Tavel, Vacqueyras and Ventoux. Some of the southern Rhone’s greatest values can be found under the Cotes du Rhone label. This is a massive region that produces vast quantities of wine and the prices are very reasonable and the wines can sometimes rival the higher priced AOC wines. There is much to question here and he begins peeling the onion and so the film builds with a quiet, dark intensity. Just a word about the cast: it’s remarkable. And there is the inestimable Eli Wallach in a cameo role as a hermit living on the Vineyard. Roman Polanski, 76, now resides in Switzerland under house arrest while a request by the U.S. for his extradition works its way through the courts. He is accused of molesting a 13-yearold girl in Los Angeles some thirty years ago and has been living as a fugitive in Europe ever since. There is something of his ordeal in the character of the P.M.: besieged, accused, and deserted by old friends. Perhaps for Polanski, The Ghost Writer is more personal than any film before, with the exception, perhaps, of The Pianist, which was extraordinary. The Ghost Writer. Pierce Brosnan delivers a top-drawer performance, as does Olivia Williams as his wife. Tom Wilkinson, always superb, portrays an Ivy League professor with a hidden past. And there is the inestimable Eli Wallach in a cameo role as a hermit living on the Vineyard. Roman Polanski, 76, now resides in Switzerland under house arrest while a request by the U.S. for his extradition works its way through the courts. He is accused of molesting a 13-yearold girl in Los Angeles some thirty years ago and has been living as a fugitive in Europe ever since. There is something of his ordeal in the character of the P.M.: besieged, accused, and deserted by old friends. Perhaps for Polanski, The Ghost Writer is more personal than any film before, with the exception, perhaps, of The Pianist, which was extraordinary. The Ghost Writer. Yet no one is particularly attractive in this film, not even a young neighbor, Wybie, who wants to befriend Coraline; in return, she accuses him of being a stalker. Young children ever so easily blur the lines between what is real and what is fantasy and might find the last half of Coraline too intense, its foreshadowed sinister edge morphing into full-blown evil. The strength of this film is that it is so wonderfully imagined. Based on Neil Gaiman’s book of the same name, which has sold over a million copies worldwide, there clearly is something about the story that resonates with kids. Another 31 programs are currently ongoing including regular monitoring and evaluation commitments, on-call technical assistance for developers, and public outreach projects. There are five programs in-progress and being worked on by City Staff which are a part of major initiatives in the Housing Element. This includes the Moraga Canyon Specific Plan, which studies all City-owned land in Moraga Canyon with the goal of creating a plan to incorporate 132-199 units of new housing. Of those units, 60 would be reserved for households earning lower incomes. Other programs include a re-examination of Commercial Uses Permitting on Grand Avenue and Highland Avenue, the city’s two commercial zones, and the development of objective design standards for 1-4 unit buildings. Thirteen programs still require further action. The City has $195,000 budgeted for professional consultants to help conduct research on various housing affordability strategies including impact fees, parcel taxes and affordable housing funds. The city provided a roadmap for the programs in 2025 that would involve significant policy decisions and were expected to come before the council in the next year. Upcoming Housing Element programs included a program to amend the City Code on the merger of lots to facilitate housing development in Piedmont’s Multi-Family Residential Zone and its Mixed Use & Commercial Zone. Of course, Disney has always been enamored with Jiminy Cricket characters like Penny (animated or otherwise) who wish upon a star, insisting it makes no difference who you are, while believing that dreams can come true. That theme is woven through countless Disney films, animated or not. And, truth be told, it’s a nice thought and has resonated with audiences for more half a century. The real treat in this film is watching Diane Lane make the character of Penny Chenery her own. Lane is a hugely gifted actress, nominated for an Oscar for her performance in Unfaithful (a tour de force film for her). She carries Secretariat from the first frame. Of course, Lane is helped by John Malkovich who portrays Lucien Laurin, the colorful French-Canadian trainer, and Margo Martindale as the longtime family secretary. Both are exceptional character actors. Malkovich’s breakthrough film was Places in the Heart; he was extraordinary. Adults will also be engaged by the sometimes sentimental yet compelling story of this remarkable horse and its equally remarkable owner. Secretariat.
